title: The Void Throne — provisional government experiment
method: Five fresh player agents plus one facilitator per test. Hard-bargaining personalities. Bounded text negotiation; nominal paper clock, not timed human play. Trial A combines later agreement, public plans and optional binding Standing Commitments. Reduced-assent Test B is conditional on failure to exercise a provisional article in A.

findings.lead: The first package produced a working provisional article under unanimous assent: Guild navigation authority in exchange for a locked month of Wayfarer service. The reduced-assent alternative was not needed for this test.
sections: The first proposal attached Lantern upkeep to Guild navigation. Daro, the Janissariat Navigation delegate, objected that this left the relief vessel free to trade. The replacement attached Wayfarer Council to the Navigation article. Both Guild owners accepted the lost trading opportunity, and GN, JN and the Ascendant all approved the article. This is the clearest evidence that a named commitment made a constitutional concession easier to accept. The run tests the combined package; it does not isolate the effect of timing from commitments.

Round two began with Guild navigation authority and an irrevocably offered Wayfarer. GN alone signed Relief; Lantern Maintain met the new upkeep duty. The Ascendant treated its navigation request as advice and chose Guard under the remaining Interim military authority. Communities recovered from 1 to 3. No resources were created and no new cooperation bonus was paid.

The Guild finished with one contract, having surrendered its second-round trading opportunity. The Ascendant surrendered navigation authority for the trial. The Janissariat accepted a quiet month, with Readiness falling from 4 to 3, while freely withholding Spear and offering Vigil. That military cost remains modest because Readiness 3 retains the strong-army threshold. Grey Petrel was never spent and all faction assets survived. Civilian losses from the first raid are recorded as civilian costs, not sacrifices by the players who ordered it.
A public plan and a binding commitment did different jobs

The final proposal paired Relief with Restraint because it also proposed military autonomy and a Vigil Home commitment. The military article failed, so its attached Vigil pledge never activated. The army subsequently offered Vigil voluntarily and the Ascendant chose Guard. The public plan could change; the activated Wayfarer assignment could not. This distinction needs to remain explicit on the paper form.

The Janissariat delegates moved from military autonomy to joint military authorisation after seeing the value of civilian Guard and of a binding say over Spear. The Ascendant accepted lasting Guild navigation in principle, citing the delivered relief, but retained its demand for imperial military command. Guild navigation plus joint military authorisation failed 4–1 at the Ceremony, with the Ascendant opposed. Guild navigation plus imperial military command then failed 3–2, with both army players opposed. The trial Navigation article expired and both domains returned to Interim. Physical recovery and the spent trading opportunity remained.
A cost that may discourage a repeat

Venn, the Guild Navigation player, explicitly warned in debrief that paying a non-refundable commercial price for authority that expired after failed ratification would make another early commitment less attractive without greater confidence in a final deal. The trial cleared the agreed uptake test, but this is a reason to test willingness again with human players. The immediate one-round power has to be worth its price even if permanent agreement fails.
The fallback gives the crown a strong bargaining position

The Ascendant stated in debrief that failure restored its governing powers, making rejection credible despite losing the shared ratification objective. Its trial concession lasted one round; the Guild could not recover the forgone contract. This asymmetry is the next issue to examine if a lasting settlement is intended to be attractive. The reduced provisional-assent option would leave the existing final-ratification rule in place.
What to carry into the next paper playtest

Retain unanimous provisional assent, negotiate after the first result, and let a faction attach one precisely named asset assignment to an article. Make the foregone choice visible beside the pledge: Wayfarer Council means no private trading voyage that month. Keep article approval and owner consent separate, and check that the commitment actually activates.

This is one fresh six-role agent run with hard-bargaining personalities, not a human playtest or a controlled comparison. Its first-round choices produced a different bargaining position from the earlier second simulation. Text exchanges were bounded and did not run against the printed 60-minute clock. Two private first-round confirmations reached their teammates verbatim only at the second-round councils; the signed assignments and public announcements had already been delivered. The facilitator records that delay. The trial does not establish that unanimity will work reliably, that both articles will be attractive, or that the full session fits its proposed timing.

GN.name: Venn
GN.temperament: Combative monopoly defender. Low willingness to compromise, high commercial risk tolerance. Treats compelled carriage as an attack on Guild independence. Will use a unilateral voyage to demonstrate leverage if credible.

GS.name: Sable
GS.temperament: Cautious contractual sceptic. Low-to-medium willingness to compromise, low personal risk tolerance. Distrusts oral assurances and military protection promises. Prefers an intact crew and explicit terms to prestige; can oppose their own teammate.

JN.name: Daro
JN.temperament: Transactional opportunist. Medium willingness to compromise, high aggression. Will offer a genuine deal but demands transport or constitutional autonomy in return. Comfortable with civilian costs if they purchase durable military power.

JS.name: Tarek
JS.temperament: Proud aggressive commander. Low willingness to compromise, high appetite for unilateral action. Hates standing down and treats Readiness loss as institutional decline. Not suicidal: can abandon an attack if shown it cannot meet an enemy.

A.name: The Sovereign
A.temperament: Authoritarian strategist. Low willingness to surrender imperial powers, high aggression, calculated risk tolerance. Uses directives and military dependence as leverage. Will share only useful vision details; would rather leave a settlement unresolved than sign away both powers cheaply.

messages.text: The petition has waited fourteen years. I prefer N-G: we accept upkeep because the route is our livelihood, while deciding which freight we carry. I prefer M-J so violence faces scrutiny and Vigil remains available for civilian protection. N-I is no settlement I would willingly recommend; recognising our licence while compelling the ship every month empties that recognition of practical value. N-J is a substantial concession, not a neutral compromise. I want both contracts if the region can survive them, our navigation team intact, and Beacon at least two. Let the crown demonstrate responsible operational choices before asking for permanent service.

messages.text: My starting preference is joint Navigation and military autonomy. We need a voice over passage and the freedom to keep Spear capable. I will bargain seriously: Guild control is tolerable if it buys an actual military lift, but an empty promise does not purchase our constitutional surrender. Our first month should demonstrate the value of soldiers who can still fight.

preferences.fallback: Consider N-G for credible passage; consider M-J only with a concrete fighting plan.

messages.text: My first preference is N-G: our discretion should carry an explicit upkeep duty, not an open-ended demand for our freight vessel. On Security I favour M-J because a Guild signature can stop an operation whose civilian cost we cannot accept. I could consider imperial command if actual protection and restraint justify it; I oppose autonomy that keeps Vigil at home while others bear the risk. Crew survival and a usable beacon matter more than a ceremonial victory. I will not pledge Lantern to Shared on an oral protection promise. Any standing commitment must name its assignment and article, and buy something concrete.

contributions.reason: Keep expertise, crews and passage viable while requiring accountable security decisions.
Autonomy and effective combat capacity are primary, while passage requires meaningful military influence.

messages.text: I want M-A: the army must decide when it fights, because leaving Spear idle makes us weaker even when every clerk calls the month peaceful. I prefer N-J over a Guild monopoly or imperial promises of passage; our delegate should have a real voice over the route. I will trade immediate service for a credible constitutional settlement, but I will not sell our future freedom merely for courteous assurances. Keep Spear intact, seek actual combat, and keep Communities above collapse. Home protects our institution; it does not cure declining conditioning. We should judge the first result before signing away anything.

My starting position is imperial priority in Navigation and imperial command in Security. The route and the fighting arm must support one government. I will consider delegation after we see the first result, but retaining at least one effective imperial power matters. I ask both factions to offer the assets needed for a protected combined operation this month; no constitutional signature is due until after its result.

messages.text: The result bought Readiness four and intact Spear at a civilian cost we must now repair. I could sign that Home commitment with JN. N-G with Lantern Maintain is negotiable if Guild delegates explicitly promise Wayfarer Council and Relief, although I prefer joint Navigation. The first result is the result I chose: the cohort is strong, but civilians paid for it and Communities one demands recovery now. I am prepared to accept A1 Navigation N-G with its attached Lantern Maintain commitment. That is a real surrender of imperial traffic priority for a reliable upkeep obligation. debrief.1_preferences_and_experience: I began and finish preferring N-G/M-J. debrief.3_actual_and_future_costs: We actually lost our second commercial contract, occupied Lantern with upkeep, and accepted an irrevocable ship assignment. Continuing upkeep was proposed final law; continuing Wayfarer service was not something I accepted. Civilians paid for the first Raid. The army offered Vigil and lost one Readiness in recovery, but four to three still left strong support: a real reduction, smaller than losing capability. Imperial Navigation authority was genuinely surrendered for round two, then restored after failed ratification.
debrief.4_exercised_and_promised: I exercised sole Navigation authority to order Relief and met N-G upkeep. The crown actually ordered Raid with Warrant, then Guard without Warrant. debrief.5_unilateral_choices_and_foresight: Trade was credible because we actually completed it without council permission. Army withholding was equally real when Spear stood down and Vigil was offered voluntarily. The Security vision made the trade-linked Raid a known opportunity, which I opposed on civilian grounds. The second Navigation vision did not justify changing Relief and could not reopen Wayfarer's lock.
debrief.6_teammate_influence: GS's first reply highlighted that reserve relief plus trade would leave Beacon one; I explicitly adopted that repair concern. GS then proposed the recovery bargain and a lost second contract. We each signed exact assignments and independently supported the later Wayfarer commitment. Our shared rejection of M-A shaped my bargaining.
debrief.7_unclear_or_objectionable: The rules ultimately made locks, duties and orders distinguishable, but repeated clarification was necessary. I object politically to paying a non-refundable operational price while final rejection removes the institutional return. That is understandable as a rule, but experience makes early commitment less attractive without stronger confidence in final agreement.
